title: Will the iPad Ever Be a Worthy Mac Replacement?
body:
iOS 9 brought us multitasking on iPad. Here's how far we've come since.
            
                        
    
                    
        
        
        
    
                                Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                            
        
        
        September 10, 2026
            
            
                        Credit: David MAREUIL/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images/Lifehacker
                            
    
        
        Welcome to a new series called Apple a Day, where sites in the CNET family are sharing pieces of Apple content from our archives—an article, review and/or video—daily from now through late September. In addition to Lifehacker, this series will include pieces from our sibling sites PCMag, Mashable, CNET and Popular Science.For the first five years of its life, the iPad could only run one app at a time. Then, iOS 9 changed everything. That update, released 10 years ago this month, introduced multitasking to the Apple tablet for the first time. "Split View" let you run two apps side-by-side at once; "Slide Over" gave you quick access to a third app in an iPhone-style window; and Picture in Picture made it possible to watch a video while working on something else. In an article published at the time, these changes prompted Lifehacker to proclaim that "iOS 9 actually makes the iPad usable for work."In total, you could have up to four different windows on screen through this concoction of features, a huge improvement over the previous limit of "one." Coupled with the new keyboard shortcuts, iOS 9 transformed the iPad, and brought it closer to the laptop replacement so many users wanted it to be. "Closer" being the key word there. 
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
Multitasking on iPad is still a work in progressWhile iOS 9 made it possible to focus on more than one app at a time, it didn't address other iPad limitations that made it difficult for computer users to fully make the switch. In the 11 years since that update, Apple has chipped away at those issues slowly but surely, while upgrading the iPad's hardware exponentially. In iOS 11, Apple made it easier to launch an app into Split View from the Dock, and introduced cross-app drag and drop. With iPadOS 13, Apple introduced a desktop-class version of Safari, and rolled out the Files app, which even supported hard drives and SD cards. iPadOS 15 improved Split View and Slide Over accessibility, and made it possible to multitask with multiple windows from one app. By iPadOS 16, it seemed like Apple had had enough of people complaining that the iPad wasn't enough like a Mac. This update introduced Stage Manager, which let users display and resize multiple floating app windows on screen. You could even connect your compatible iPad to an external monitor to run Stage Manager on both displays, just as you might connect a MacBook to a monitor. iPadOS 17 improved the experience again, adding support for FaceTime calls from external webcams, while last year's iPadOS 26 provided another overhaul, introducing the closest thing to a macOS-like window system yet, right down to the traffic-light window buttons. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
We're at the point where, on the surface, the iPad can be considered Apple's answer to the touchscreen computer, especially when paired with a keyboard and trackpad. But in practical use, it's evident the iPad still isn't a Mac, even in cases where the iPad supports the apps and utilities you use on Mac. iPadOS doesn't feel designed for computer tasks; it feels like computer tasks were retrofitted to iPadOS. That doesn't mean things like multitasking and file support aren't welcome features, but the experience isn't as refined as it is on macOS. What's more, there is evidence Apple agrees the two devices are just too different, as rumors suggest the company might release a touchscreen MacBook as soon as next year. For me, iPadOS still feels at its best when I use one app at a time. All the above efforts to change its nature aside, that's probably because the iPad was originally designed that way. 
            
                        
                
            
                    
                                            
                
            
                Jake Peterson
                                    Senior Technology Editor
                                
                                            Covering tech news, how-to guides, explainers, and more.

title: How to Get the Most Cloud Storage Possible for Free
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 15, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit:  Ian Moore/Lifehacker/Getty Images
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Cloud storage is likely an essential part of your data management strategy, whether you're just using Google Drive for documents or you back up everything to a remote service. You can get a significant amount of space for a reasonable monthly fee, but if you prefer not to pay, it's possible to combine free options and cobble together quite a bit of free storage—around 80GB (or more)—at no cost. A reminder: You shouldn't rely solely on cloud storage for your backups. Follow the 3-2-1 rule, which protects against a single point of failure, such as getting locked out of your account or issues with the service itself. Google: 15GB of free cloud storageThe most obvious option for free storage is Google Drive. Google offers up to 15GB of storage per account, though this is split across all Google apps, including Gmail, Google Drive, and Google Photos as well as Android backups. You could create multiple Google accounts, which would allow you to stack 15GB allotments. Note that Google recently introduced a 5GB free storage cap on some new accounts, though you can get around this by linking a phone number. 
Apple iCloud: 5GB of free cloud storageiCloud users automatically get 5GB of free storage, split across backups, photos, and files, as well as data from Messages, Mail, Contacts, FaceTime, voice memos, and Apple Invites. You can delete content to reduce the size of your iCloud backup to manage available storage space. The cheapest paid iCloud+ tier comes with 50GB storage for around $1 per month. Microsoft OneDrive: 5GB of free cloud storageSimilar to iCloud, OneDrive comes with 5GB of free cloud storage, and all you need is a Microsoft 365 account. This limit is shared across documents, files, and photos—Outlook gets a separate 15GB allotment. Box: 10GB of free cloud storageBox offers 10GB of secure storage on its free plan. There's a 250GB file upload limit, so this isn't the best option for media or larger files, plus you only get access to one file version. Free users do get 5 e-signature requests per month, so Box is a good choice for documents. Dropbox: 2GB of free cloud storageDropbox's free plan is limited to just 2GB of storage, which can be filled with photos, documents, and files from up to three devices. You can also use Dropbox to share files and collaborate with other users, and the service integrates with many third-party apps. Proton Drive: 5GB of free cloud storageProton is known for its privacy-focused products, so Proton Drive is a good choice for storing sensitive records like tax returns and legal documents. The free plan comes with 5GB of space, and your vault is end-to-end encrypted. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
MEGA: 20GB of free cloud storageMEGA allows a whopping 20GB of storage to free users with automatic backups and 100 file versions, making it a solid option for large archives and media. Other cloud storage services: Free storage amounts varyThere are a handful of other cloud storage providers that offer free plans without aggressive ads, major file size limitations, or serious privacy compromises. Other options include Sync.com (5GB), Icedrive (10GB), and pCloud (up to 10GB), though some users on Reddit have noted reliability and customer support concerns with these services. Password managers often include free storageYour password manager subscription may not technically be free, but if you're already paying for it, you may have some small amount of secure file storage at no additional cost. Bitwarden's Premium plan comes with 5 GB of encrypted storage, while many others (1Password, Proton Pass, and Dashlane, to name a few) include 1 GB. How to organize and maximize your free storage spaceIf you are using multiple cloud storage services, you can distribute different content types across each to maximize features and ease of access. Proton Drive and Sync.com are good choices for sensitive files you want to be sure are secure, though you can use a tool like Cryptomator (which is free and open source) to encrypt your vault before syncing to a service like Google Drive or Box. Google Drive, OneDrive, and iCloud are best for files and documents you need regularly, including items that require collaboration and sharing, as well as device backups. MEGA could be a solid option for cold storage—media that doesn't change or need to be accessed often. And Box is useful for smaller documents, like PDF records and receipts, given its individual file size limit.

        Proton VPN’s latest promotion offers its two-year VPN Plus plan for $2.99 per month (down from $9.99), a 70% discount that saves you $168 over the introductory term. Meanwhile, NetShield blocks known ad, tracking, and malware domains, helping prevent some unwanted resources from loading without guaranteeing ad-free streaming or protection against every threat.         Samsung’s flagship soundbars have reached the point where the yearly upgrades are more about refinement than reinvention, and that is pretty much the story with the Samsung HW-Q990H. Right now, this 2026 model is down to $1,049.99 on Woot, which is its lowest price yet, according to price trackers. The same system is listed on Amazon for $1,697.99 (down from $1,997.99), so not only is the discount substantial, but Prime members also get free shipping (everyone else pays a $6 delivery fee).
Samsung kept the same 11.1.4-channel setup from the older HW-Q990F, including the soundbar, wireless subwoofer, and two rear speakers, but leaned harder into software this time around—features like the SpaceFit Sound Pro automatically adjust the sound depending on your room layout, and unlike some auto-calibration features that barely change anything, this one reportedly shifts the audio balance in noticeable ways. Sometimes it improves dialogue clarity and bass response. Other times, you may prefer tweaking things yourself with the built-in seven-band EQ. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The system also handles basically every major audio format, supports wireless Dolby Atmos with compatible Samsung TVs, and includes 4K 120Hz HDMI passthrough for people gaming on a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X. That said, while the bass is strong for a compact subwoofer, it compresses when you push the volume near maximum, so it's not perfect for huge spaces or people who want nightclub-level output. More importantly, if you already own the HW-Q990F or even the older HW-Q990D, upgrading probably will not feel dramatic enough to justify the cost. But for someone starting from TV speakers or an entry-level soundbar, this system can completely change how movies, games, and even sports feel at home.

        If you want an advanced fitness tracker in a sleek package, Garmin makes some of the best options for detailed health and workout insights, along with longer battery life than many mainstream smartwatches. One of its most enticing models is the Garmin Vivoactive 6, which is currently down to a record-low $229.99 (originally $299.99) on Amazon.
Its 1.2-inch AMOLED touchscreen is crisp and easier to read than Garmin’s older display technology. It’s also lightweight at 36 grams with the included band and slim, at just 10.9 mm thick. As a result, it’s a better option for overnight wear and sleep tracking than the bulkier Venu. The watch also has a Smart Wake Alarm, which uses a half-hour window to try to wake you during a lighter sleep stage with vibration, giving users a more pleasant way to wake up than a blaring phone alarm.  The watch lasts up to 11 days in smartwatch mode, removing the need to charge it nightly, and it delivers up to 21 hours of battery life in GPS-only mode. Built-in GPS lets you accurately track outdoor workouts and activities without bringing your phone, while music storage allows for phone-free listening with compatible Bluetooth headphones. It also features Garmin Pay for contactless payments, so you can leave your wallet behind, too.With more than 80 preloaded sports apps, the Vivoactive 6 is highly versatile and supports a wide range of workouts. It’s also a solid option for strength training, with tools to track reps, sets, and rest periods, plus step-by-step workouts for strength, HIIT, yoga, Pilates, mobility, and more. Beyond health and fitness tracking, it includes Garmin Coach plans that adapt to your performance and health metrics, plus daily suggested workouts.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
It doesn’t have every feature serious runners and adventurers may want from the brand’s pricier watches, such as more advanced training and navigation tools. But it packs a ton of useful features into a lightweight, everyday-friendly design and lets you spend more time away from your phone if that’s the goal. At $70 off, the Garmin Vivoactive 6 is a great choice for iPhone and Android users who want a capable fitness smartwatch without the premium Garmin price tag.

title: Yes, the Apple Watch's New Audio Intelligence Features Really Are Always Listening to You
description: During its Sept. 9 keynote, Apple announced the Apple Watch Series 12 and the Ultra 4, both of which will come with a feature that p
body:
During its Sept. 9 keynote, Apple announced the Apple Watch Series 12 and the Ultra 4, both of which will come with a feature that passively listens to your audio conversations all day and can summarize them for you on demand. It's part of a collection of features called "Audio Intelligence," but the two key features to consider here are: Live Rewind: If you double-press the Digital Crown on your Apple Watch, it will pull up a text snippet of your conversation over the last fifteen seconds. Siri Recaps: Your watch listens to your conversations and generates an AI summary of any of your transcribed audio at the end of each day. At first glance, the basic concept seems like a privacy nightmare, but Apple has put some safeguards in place to help people feel more comfortable with this feature: The audio that is captured is never recorded or stored, and never leaves your device; it is essentially deleted immediately and in real time from local storage; only a truncated version is uploaded to Apple Private Cloud Compute servers for AI processing, and the resulting transcript that is delivered to you is end-to-end encrypted.Still, there are some potential privacy concerns worth considering, especially since you'll essentially be subjecting everyone around you to using it without their consent.
How Audio Intelligence makes a transcript of what it hearsSeries 12 and Ultra 4 watches run on an S11 chip with a Secure Exclave feature, a partitioned local storage compartment that even the operating system cannot access. When your Apple Watch picks up ambient audio, it is sent straight into this protected buffer, where it is encrypted, then sent over to a matching Secure Enclave on your paired iPhone. From there, your iPhone transcribes it locally using an on-device AI model to create a summarized version that’s half the length of the actual audio, removing everything but the essentials, and stripping out any identifying information. After the audio data is overwritten, the transcript is sent to Apple's Private Cloud Compute along with some generic metadata, like a rough location and timestamps. None of the audio data is tied to your Apple ID once it reaches the servers at this stage. Apple uses a third-party relay to conceal your IP address while uploading the data to Private Cloud Compute, so not even their employees can identify you from your device. While in the Private Cloud Compute servers, your audio data gets summarized by Siri AI. This is how you end up with daily text summaries of your audio, provided you opt into Siri Recap. Siri Recap summaries are auto-deleted every seven days unless you choose to save them individually. All of this might seem perfectly secure, but here comes the risky part: If you choose to save a conversation summary with Siri Recap, that data is uploaded to your iCloud storage and can even be saved in apps like Apple Notes or Journal. Server-level data breaches at companies like Apple are rare, but account-level hacks happen more often than you might think: 900,000 compromised iCloud logins were found sitting on a public server after a data leak just this January. If someone manages to hack into your Apple ID or access your unsecured iPhone, they might be able to view all your saved conversation summaries from a single place. And it’s not just the potential data breach that should scare you, but all the associated privacy concerns.
    
            
            Series 12 and Ultra 4 watches will now come loaded with Apple's new audio intelligence feature 
                                        Credit: Apple
                    
    
A potential privacy nightmareApple has spent a lot of time thinking through ways to protect its customers when they use the Audio Intelligence feature, but none of these protections extend to other people who might be sitting across the table or in the same room as you. To its credit, Apple has added an audio chime and a brief visual cue that plays on your watch whenever the Live Rewind feature is triggered. This is intended to inform people around you that they are being listened to. Live Rewind also doesn’t identify speakers, so it won’t name or otherwise identify the person speaking in the transcriptions or summaries—but none of that actually prevents people from being eavesdropped on without their explicit consent. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Siri Recap’s implementation is arguably even worse. It has no audio or visual cues to indicate that it’s running, so no one knows that they are being surveilled if you enable this feature. Apple’s privacy documentation is visibly scarce when it comes to the issue of consent, apart from a vague warning on the product pages that advises you to “be mindful of those around you.” This is a potential concern not just for other people who might worry about being spied on every time they see an Apple Watch, but also Apple Watch users themselves, if they are in a region where local laws require consent before recording audio: Some 12 U.S. states have explicit all-party consent laws that forbid undisclosed recordings, while outside the U.S., many E.U. countries have instituted similar requirements; the E.U.'s GDPR also prohibits recordings containing personally identifiable information without disclosure. Using an Apple Watch with the Audio Intelligence feature enabled might sound like it would put you in violation of these laws, but at this point, it seems the device operates in a bit of a grey area—as Apple's privacy documentation notes: Audio Intelligence features do not create audio recordings that can be accessedby the operating system, apps, the user, or Apple. There is no recording to share,forward, or produce if requested by any party, because no recording exists.The Secure Exclave buffer where the audio is initially processed is "a continuously overwritten stream that exists only within the protected hardware and never creates an audio recording," Apple says, meaning no one needs to consent to being recorded. In theory. But that Apple felt the need to go into great detail to explain how the feature technically doesn't violate any privacy laws probably doesn't make it feel any less dystopian to those inclined to view it that way.How to turn Audio Intelligence on or offGiven all the potential security concerns, it’s a good thing that Apple has at least made its Audio Intelligence features opt-in only. They won’t be enabled by default on your new Apple Watch, and you can choose to enable or disable individual features as you choose to. Here's what to look for:Sound Recognition: Open the Settings app on your iPhone. Navigate to Accessibility > Sound & Name Recognition > Sound Recognition. Here you can toggle the “Detect using Apple Watch” option on or off. Music Recognition: Open the Settings app directly on your Apple Watch. Tap on Smart Stack. Switch "Music Detection" on or off per your needs. Live Rewind: Open the Watch app on your iPhone. Go to Siri > Live Rewind. You can choose to enable or disable “Double Click Digital Crown” to control this feature. Siri Recap: Again on the Watch app on your iPhone, go to Siri > Siri Recap. You can enable or disable the feature here, or even set an autorun schedule for it if you like. Siri Recap can also be switched on and off by flipping a single toggle in your Control Center.

title: 10 Hacks Every Libby User Should Know
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 10, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Ian Moore/Lifehacker/Getty Images/Libby
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Libby is a service that connects users to their local library systems, giving them access to an enormous catalog of digital content, including e-books, audiobooks, and magazines—for free. If you're a reader (or listener), you'll want to take advantage of these Libby tips and tricks for borrowing, organizing, and maximizing your loans. Add multiple library cards to see availability across other systemsYou're not limited to one library system on Libby. The platform allows you to connect to multiple libraries, so you can take advantage of larger catalogs in case one library has more titles or a shorter wait times for books you want to read. You still have to be eligible for a library card at every library you connect to, but you could add your city library, your county library, and a school library to your account (or even take advantage of a friend's or family member's card from a different city). Go to Menu > Add Library and search by library name, city, or zip code. Select the library to browse its collection, and follow the prompts to add that library's card if you qualify. Use airplane mode on your Kindle to extend your loan Libby automatically returns titles as soon as your loans expire, so unlike with physical books, you can't take extra time to finish up. But if you're reading on a Kindle, you may be able to borrow the title and immediately set your device to airplane mode to freeze the loan. While your Kindle is offline, you can return the title via the Libby app so the next person can borrow it. Note that there are reports that this workaround, which is unique to Kindle, may no longer be available on newer devices running the latest software, but Reddit users suggest that changing the date on your Kindle to before the return deadline and/or keeping the expired book open could also help avoid this issue. 
Export your reading data to archive or add it to Goodreads If you like to track your reading history, you can export a timeline of your activity, which can be saved in a personal spreadsheet or uploaded to Goodreads. Tap Shelf > Timeline > Actions > Export Timeline and choose a format—Table creates a shareable HTML page, while Spreadsheet downloads an editable sheet to your device (JSON is also an option). Exports include information like the title name, author, borrow date, publisher, and ISBN. If syncing to Goodreads, choose Spreadsheet and follow the platform's import instructions. Libby's tag system makes it easy to organize and sort titles across multiple lists, such as annual reading lists, favorites, or TBR (to name a few). Simply go to Tags > Actions > New Tag, add a name and description, and tap Create. When you want to add a title to one of these lists, hit Save on the title's page and select all relevant tags. Tap Tags on the bottom navigation to sort or filter tagged titles. Set up notifications to get first access to new releases Not all new releases are immediately available to every library system, but you can get a head start on borrowing with the "Notify Me" smart tag, which will alert you when your library adds titles you've tagged. When you find a title via search that your library doesn't offer, you'll be prompted to create a Notify Me tag. You can also manually create one by following the process for custom tags and selecting Notify Me to turn it into a smart tag. This tag also works for new magazine issues and new content from specific authors or book series. Make sure you have push notifications enabled for Libby. If you finish one book and want to immediately start another, you can use a search filter to find titles that are available now rather than sorting through wait lists. Then, you can pin that filter so every search—even if other filters are applied—shows you only titles that are ready to borrow. Go to Search and tap the three horizontal lines to open the filter list. Select available now > Show Titles, then press and hold the filter to open the pop-up menu and tap Pin Filter. You can follow the same process with other filters (if you only want to see books and/or audiobooks, for example). Note that subject filters can't be pinned. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Adjust your download settings to manage storage spaceAudiobooks can be storage hogs, and if you're listening to more than one title at a time, you may not want to devote that much of your device's space to those files. Customize how titles are downloaded versus streamed via Menu > Settings > Download Rules, where you can choose whether to automatically download everything, nothing, or only titles under 20 MB as well as enable downloads on wifi only (to avoid mobile data usage). Revisit your highlights and notes in your reading journey or Read.Amazon If you like to highlight passages or add notes to books as you read, you can review these annotations for titles borrowed via Libby even after you've returned them. In the Libby app, find the title and tap the cover image, then tap Reading Journey. You can also export these data via Actions > Export Reading Data. If you read the title on a Kindle device, notes and highlights are also saved on Amazon and visible on Goodreads. Search for skip-the-line books to bypass wait timesPopular titles and new releases often rack up hundreds of holds in a short amount of time, meaning you could be waiting months before a copy is available at your library. Some library systems will designate a few copies of these books as "skip the line," meaning that they can't be reserved or renewed and instead are claimed on a first-come-first-serve basis once returned by the previous user. These titles are marked with a shamrock icon, and if your library offers them, you can find them via Search > Catalog Filters > skip the line. Use the Suspend feature to stagger overlapping holdsIf you have a long list of holds with varying wait times, you may occasionally have one or more books ready to borrow around the same time. If you're not ready to read a title as soon as it becomes available, you can opt to suspend your hold until you're done with the book you're currently reading or have more time to start something new. This keeps your place in line, so the book will be yours as soon as you un-suspend your hold and the title is returned by the current user. In the app, go to Shelf > Holds > Manage Hold > Suspend Hold, or tap Suspend next to the title if it is ready to borrow.

title: I Tried 'Tailscale,' the Self-Hosted VPN Service That Makes It Look Like You're Always Home
body:
David Nield
                            
        
            David Nield
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceDavid Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years. He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 15, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Tailscale has apps for all the major device platforms.
                                                    Credit: Tailscale
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Tailscale wasn't on my radar until a friend recently raved about its capabilities to me. Looking around the web, it seems the software has attracted a loyal following; perhaps part of the reason I hadn't come across it before is that it's not all that easy to understand what it does. Tailscale is technically a VPN (Virtual Private Network), but not in the way the term is typically used. Whereas something like NordVPN or ExpressVPN connects you to someone else's network to access the wider web, Tailscale does the opposite, and connects you to your own network from outside.
    
            
            Start your tailnet with one of the apps.
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
"Remote access technology" has been around for years, of course, but it often involves a lot of detailed and technical setup steps—you want to be able to access your home network remotely without letting anyone else in, and that usually means some complicated configuration involving router settings and several third-party apps.There's none of that with Tailscale, and when you actually install the software, you quickly start to see what all the fuss is about. You can be sitting in a coffee shop or hotel room and have virtually the same access to your home network as you would if you were actually in your living room, which has all kinds of benefits, from file sharing to managing your smart home devices.
The obvious use case is remote access to a computer you have at home, without the layers of complexity or using another company's servers. Tailscale also makes it easier to access media servers you've set up with apps like Plex or Jellyfin, and smart home setups running through Home Assistant or another dashboard.
    
            
            You can be set up in minutes.
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
Everything is built on the open-source WireGuard VPN protocol, which creates private and encrypted links to all of the devices you want to connect to your network—your "tailnet." To add a new device, just install Tailscale on it, whether it's your phone on a 5G connection or a desktop computer set up at the office. Tailscale is free for personal use, which covers up to six individual users and an unlimited number of personal devices, though there are some limits: 50 tagged resources (always-on devices that need multi-user access, like a NAS box), and three Access Control List or ACL groups (for setting access permissions per user). Paid plans start at $8 per month.Putting Tailscale to the testThe ease of setup is one of the main appeals of Tailscale, and it couldn't be much more straightforward. Download the relevant app on whatever device you want to start with, create an account (you can sign in using a Google, Microsoft, GitHub, or Apple account), and you're up and running. I had a Windows PC, a MacBook, an Android phone, and an iPhone connected to my tailnet in a matter of minutes, with just a few taps and clicks required. There's also a web portal you can access to see all of the devices you've connected and what they're up to.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        

    
            
            The macOS app offers easy drag-and-drop file sharing.
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
One improvement I noticed right away was the addition of Tailscale to the share sheet on Android and iOS, which meant I could quickly share photos and other files between all my devices in seconds (no AirDrop or Android Quick Share required). I could also instantly access the shared folders on my desktop and laptop computers from my phone.Something else you can do very easily is set up a remote access app on a phone and use it to connect directly to one of your computers in a different physical location, with no exposure to the wider internet and no advanced configuration required—Tailscale provides you with an IP address that looks like a local network. Any of your home computers can be configured as an exit node as well, which means internet traffic can be rerouted through it. If you're in a hotel, for example, you can use Tailscale as a secure tunnel back home, which means websites see you as visiting from home rather than an unrecognized hotel IP address.
    
            
            Taildrop lets you quickly share files between connected devices.
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
There are some areas where Tailscale can improve (the Windows client isn't quite as straightforward to use as the macOS one), and it's fair to say at least some basic networking knowledge is required to get to grips with Tailscale, but in terms of software that's free and useful, it's hard to beat. I didn't dive into more advanced use cases involving NAS drives or home servers, as they're not something that I'm working with at the moment, but that's the next level of Tailscale capability

        The Pixel Watch 4 may no longer be Google’s newest smartwatch, now that the Pixel Watch 5 has taken its place, but it's only been on the market for a short time and is already seeing a substantial discount—the matte-black 45mm LTE model is currently $379.99, down from $499.99, while the smaller 41mm LTE version has fallen from $449.99 to $329.99. Both are $120 off and sitting at their lowest prices to date, according to price trackers. Meanwhile, the 41mm LTE Pixel Watch 5 is currently $100 off, bringing its price down to $399.99 from $499.99. That's just $20 more than the 45mm LTE Pixel Watch 4, if you want the latest Pixel Watch on the market.
The Pixel Watch 4 is positioned as Google’s premium wearable—its circular display is larger than before and can hit up to 3,000 nits of brightness, so it stays readable outdoors without much effort. Plus, the LTE model adds some independence from your phone, including the ability to send satellite SOS messages if you are out of cellular range. Dual-band GPS also improves location tracking, especially in crowded cities or areas with weak signals.Day-to-day use feels focused on speed and convenience. Charging is one of the standout improvements here. You can go from empty to full in about 30 minutes, and even a quick 15-minute top-up gets you to around 50%. That makes it easier to wear the watch all day and still track sleep at night without planning around long charging breaks. That said, while battery life is solid, daily charging will still be part of the routine.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Most of the core experience will feel familiar if you have used a recent Pixel Watch—including built-in Gemini for voice commands, along with a full set of health sensors such as heart rate, blood oxygen, temperature tracking, and sleep monitoring. Fitness tracking is reliable for runs, walks, and gym sessions, though it still leans more toward general wellness than advanced sports metrics. In all, this is a well-rounded Android smartwatch, and it makes sense if you want a watch that looks good and stays easy to live with.
